question.prompt:
The \(8 \times 18\) rectangle \(ABCD\) is cut into two congruent hexagons, as shown, in such a way that the two hexagons can be repositioned without overlap to form a square. What is \(y?\)

[Figure 1](figures/2006_AMC_12A_Q06_question_fig1.svg)

solutions.explanation:
[Figure 1](figures/2006_AMC_12A_Q06_question_fig1.svg)

Repositioning the pieces preserves their total area. The square therefore has area \(8\cdot18=144\), so its positive side length is \(12\).

We now determine how the pieces can cover the square's corners. Each L-shaped hexagon spans the full \(8\)-unit height of the original rectangle. When the pieces form the square, their edges align with the square's sides: the square's boundary uses piece edges, and the shared boundary aligns the two pieces' perpendicular edge directions.

Because each piece has a span of \(8<12\) in one direction, it cannot contain three square corners or two opposite square corners. The four corners must therefore be covered by two adjacent corners from each piece. Those adjacent corners are \(12\) units apart, so each piece's other span, horizontal in the original rectangle, must be \(12\).

Thus the left piece extends \(12\) units from \(AD\), placing the cut's endpoint on \(AB\) at distance \(12\) from \(A\). The right piece extends \(12\) units from \(BC\), placing the cut's endpoint on \(DC\) at distance \(18-12=6\) from \(D\). The horizontal step is the difference between these positions:
\[
y=12-6=6.
\]
The answer is \(\boxed{6}\), choice \(\mathrm{A}\).
solutions.title: Area and corner spans
